title: Levitated Milligram-scale Ferromagnetic Magnetometer at Room Temperature
authors: Yuanji Sheng, Kenan Tian, Rui Li, Yiming Chen, Dingjiang Long, Siwen Chen, Peiran Yin
abstract: Levitated mechanical oscillators are emerging ultrasensitive sensors with tremendous potential in both applied and fundamental physics. Levitated ferromagnets, with internal spin noises rapidly averaged, promise ultrahigh magnetic sensitivity. Here, we demonstrate a milligram-scale diamagnetically levitated ferromagnet system operating at room temperature. Through optimized geometry and multi-channel dissipation control, we achieve a magnetic sensitivity of 23~fT$/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ at frequency of 100-Hz level. We anticipate that a ferromagnetic magnetometer with subfemtotesla sensitivity is within reach, after modest technical improvements. This platform establishes a high-performance magnetometer for biomagnetic field detection and beyond-standard-model force searches.
summary: The research demonstrates a room-temperature magnetometer using a levitated ferromagnet achieving 23 fT/sqrt(Hz) sensitivity. By carefully controlling dissipation mechanisms like eddy currents and hysteresis loss, the system establishes a high-performance sensor for detecting weak magnetic fields in applications ranging from biomedicine to fundamental physics searches.
main_problem: Developing ultrasensitive magnetic field sensors by utilizing levitated ferromagnetic oscillators at room temperature for applications like biomagnetic detection and beyond-standard-model force searches.
main_result: The authors achieved a magnetic sensitivity of 23 fT/sqrt(Hz) at the 100 Hz level, matching state-of-the-art cryogenic systems.
method: Magnetic field sensitivity was calibrated using direct optical rotation angle measurement and applied periodic magnetic field excitation on a levitated system.
model_or_system: The platform is a milligram-scale diamagnetically levitated ferromagnet suspended in an environment stabilized by PID control. Its motion dynamics are governed by the equation I d^2(theta)/dt^2 + I*gamma*d(theta)/dt + I*omega_0^2 * theta = tau_signal + tau_noise.
key_observables: Magnetic field sensitivity (S_BB), angular displacement PSD, and mechanical damping rates ($\gamma$).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation; 23 fT/sqrt(Hz) sensitivity; resonant frequency near 153 Hz.
main_assumptions: Future enhancements rely on further suppression of vibration noises and magnetic hysteresis loss.
figures_summary: Figures show the experimental setup schematic, simulated field distributions, PSDs of rotation angles, and ringdown measurements demonstrating mechanical damping.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical system (levitated ferromagnet), analyzes the governing dynamics and noise sources (dissipation mechanisms like eddy currents and hysteresis loss), presents measurement techniques, and reports achieving a high sensitivity benchmark.
why_interesting: This work bridges classical mechanical sensing with quantum-limited noise analysis, providing an experimental platform for ultra-sensitive measurements relevant to fundamental physics searches beyond standard models.

Two layers of ferrite magnetic shield outside the PEEK frame are used to shield external magnetic field noises and suppress eddy currents generated in metallic conductors. Figure 2(b) displays ringdown measurements of x-axis rotational energy decay at different pressures. At a pres- sure of 8.6 × 10−2 mbar (denoted as high pressure), the measured decay time constant is 36.2 s, consistent with the Lorentzian-fitted mechanical dissipation γlow/2π in Fig. 2(a). At this high pressure, the mechanical dissi- pation are dominated by the background gas. Reducing pressure to 6.4 × 10−5 mbar (denoted as low pressure) yields a limiting decay constant of 324.3 s, corresponding to γhigh/2π = 0.49 mHz, Q = 3.1 × 105. This dissipation rate is verified to be pressure-independent.
